topic: IoT Telemetry Ingestion & Streaming Analytics Pipeline
question: For this question, refer to the TerramEarth case study. TerramEarth's CTO wants to use the raw data from connected vehicles to help identify approximately when a vehicle in the field will experience a component failure. You want to allow analysts to centrally query the vehicle data. Which architecture should you recommend?
stem: For this question, refer to the TerramEarth case study. TerramEarth's CTO wants to use the raw data from connected vehicles to help identify approximately when a vehicle in the field will experience a component failure. You want to allow analysts to centrally query the vehicle data. Which architecture should you recommend?
options: IoT device -> Google Cloud Load Balancing -> Google Kubernetes Engine -> Cloud Pub/Sub -> Cloud Dataflow -> BigQuery -> analysis
IoT device -> App Engine flexible environment -> Cloud Pub/Sub -> Cloud Dataflow -> BigQuery -> analysis
IoT device -> Cloud Storage -> Cloud Dataproc -> Cloud SQL -> analysis
IoT device -> Cloud VPN -> Compute Engine FTP servers -> Cloud Bigtable -> analysis
hint: Use Google Cloud Load Balancing in front of GKE to terminate custom/legacy vehicle ingestion protocols before buffering in Pub/Sub, processing with Dataflow, and querying in BigQuery.
explanation: Both leading architectures use the Google-recommended real-time streaming analytics pipeline: Cloud Pub/Sub for global message buffering, Cloud Dataflow for streaming ETL transformation, and BigQuery for centralized SQL analysis. However, because TerramEarth's existing connected fleet uploads gzipped CSV telemetry over custom FTP connections, the ingestion front door must efficiently handle non-HTTP protocols at massive connection concurrency. Google Cloud Load Balancing in front of Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) containers provides full Layer 4 networking flexibility and autoscaling for custom protocol servers, whereas App Engine flexible environment is optimized for HTTP(S) web traffic.

whyWrong.1: App Engine flexible environment is optimized for HTTP/HTTPS web services rather than high-volume custom FTP protocol termination from hundreds of thousands of vehicles.
whyWrong.2: Cloud SQL is a regional relational database that cannot scale to store or run analytical queries across multi-terabyte daily vehicle telemetry.
whyWrong.3: Relying on Cloud VPN and Cloud Bigtable fails to provide SQL-based central analytical querying for business analysts.

stem: For this question, refer to the TerramEarth case study. The TerramEarth development team wants to create an API to meet the company's business requirements. You want the development team to focus their development effort on business value versus creating a custom framework. Which method should they use?
options: Use Google App Engine with a JAX-RS Jersey Java-based framework. Focus on an API for the public.
Use Google App Engine with Google Cloud Endpoints. Focus on an API for dealers and partners.
Use Google App Engine with the Swagger (OpenAPI Specification) framework. Focus on an API for the public.
Use Google Kubernetes Engine with a Django Python container. Focus on an API for the public.
Use Google Kubernetes Engine with a Tomcat container with the Swagger (OpenAPI Specification) framework. Focus on an API for dealers and partners.
hint: Combine serverless App Engine with Cloud Endpoints to eliminate infrastructure and API gateway boilerplate while targeting TerramEarth's actual B2B audience (dealers and partners).
explanation: TerramEarth's explicit business requirements state that the API must support the dealer network with equipment usage data and enable partnerships with seed and fertilizer suppliers—not general public consumers. Pairing serverless Google App Engine with Cloud Endpoints provides managed authentication, API key management, monitoring, and OpenAPI spec enforcement out of the box so developers can focus strictly on business logic rather than managing Kubernetes clusters or custom frameworks.

whyWrong.0: Targeting the general public violates TerramEarth's business requirements, which specify dealers and agricultural partners as the API consumers.
whyWrong.2: Targeting the public is incorrect per the case study requirements, and Cloud Endpoints provides managed gateway capabilities beyond raw OpenAPI specs.
whyWrong.3: Running GKE introduces unnecessary container orchestration overhead and targets the wrong audience (public instead of dealers and partners).
whyWrong.4: Although targeting dealers and partners is right, managing Tomcat containers on GKE adds significant operational overhead compared to serverless App Engine with Cloud Endpoints.

topic: Delegated Authorization with OAuth 2.0
question: For this question, refer to the TerramEarth case study. Your development team has created a structured API to retrieve vehicle data. They want to allow third parties to develop tools for dealerships that use this vehicle event data. You want to support delegated authorization against this data. What should you do?
stem: For this question, refer to the TerramEarth case study. Your development team has created a structured API to retrieve vehicle data. They want to allow third parties to develop tools for dealerships that use this vehicle event data. You want to support delegated authorization against this data. What should you do?
options: Restrict data access based on the source IP address of the partner systems.
Build SAML 2.0 SSO compatibility into your authentication system.
Build or leverage an OAuth-compatible access control system.
Create secondary credentials for each dealer that can be given to the trusted third party.
hint: OAuth 2.0 is the industry-standard protocol specifically designed for delegated authorization without sharing user passwords or credentials.
explanation: Delegated authorization enables a resource owner (a TerramEarth dealership) to grant a third-party application scoped, time-limited, and revocable access to their vehicle telemetry API without sharing their primary credentials. OAuth 2.0 is specifically designed for delegated authorization via scoped access tokens. SAML 2.0 handles federated user authentication (SSO), not third-party API delegation, while sharing secondary credentials or relying on source IP allowlists violates zero-trust and least-privilege principles.

whyWrong.1: SAML 2.0 is an enterprise Single Sign-On (SSO) authentication standard for verifying user identity, not a protocol for delegated third-party API authorization.
whyWrong.0: IP address allowlisting cannot distinguish between individual dealerships or enforce fine-grained, user-revocable data scopes.
whyWrong.3: Sharing static secondary credentials with third parties violates security best practices, prevents granular scoping, and makes credential rotation and revocation difficult.

topic: High-Throughput Global IoT Ingestion
question: For this question, refer to the TerramEarth case study. TerramEarth plans to connect all 20 million vehicles in the field to the cloud. This increases the volume to 20 million 600-byte records a second for 40 TB an hour. How should you design the data ingestion?
stem: For this question, refer to the TerramEarth case study. TerramEarth plans to connect all 20 million vehicles in the field to the cloud. This increases the volume to 20 million 600-byte records a second for 40 TB an hour. How should you design the data ingestion?
options: Vehicles write data directly to Google Cloud Storage (GCS).
Vehicles continue to write data using the existing system (FTP).
Vehicles stream data directly to Google BigQuery.
Vehicles write data directly to Google Cloud Pub/Sub.
hint: Cloud Pub/Sub is Google Cloud's globally distributed, horizontally autoscaling ingestion buffer engineered for millions of small event writes per second.
explanation: Ingesting 20 million 600-byte records per second (12 GB/s or ~40 TB/hour) from globally distributed vehicles requires a globally available, low-latency, durable messaging service that decouples edge producers from downstream processing pipelines. Google Cloud Pub/Sub automatically scales to millions of messages per second across global points of presence and buffers spikes safely before Dataflow processes and loads the data into BigQuery.

whyWrong.0: Cloud Storage is an object store optimized for larger blobs and batch files; writing 20 million tiny 600-byte objects per second incurs extreme request overhead and cost.
whyWrong.2: Directly streaming 20 million unbuffered records per second from edge vehicles into BigQuery bypasses ingestion decoupling, validation, and cost optimization.
whyWrong.1: Legacy FTP servers cannot scale to 20 million concurrent vehicle streams and were the root cause of TerramEarth's 3-week reporting lag.

topic: Process Transformation for Predictive Maintenance
question: For this question, refer to the TerramEarth case study. You analyzed TerramEarth's business requirement to reduce downtime and found that they can achieve a majority of time saving by reducing customers' wait time for parts. You decided to focus on reduction of the 3-week aggregate reporting time. Which modifications to the company's processes should you recommend?
stem: For this question, refer to the TerramEarth case study. You analyzed TerramEarth's business requirement to reduce downtime and found that they can achieve a majority of time saving by reducing customers' wait time for parts. You decided to focus on reduction of the 3-week aggregate reporting time. Which modifications to the company's processes should you recommend?
options: Increase fleet cellular connectivity to 80%, migrate from FTP to streaming transport, and develop machine learning analysis of metrics.
Migrate from FTP to streaming transport, migrate from CSV to binary format, and develop machine learning analysis of metrics.
Migrate from CSV to binary format, migrate from FTP to SFTP transport, and develop machine learning analysis of metrics.
Migrate from FTP to SFTP transport, develop machine learning analysis of metrics, and increase dealer local inventory by a fixed factor.
hint: A real-time streaming pipeline only eliminates the 3-week reporting delay if the vehicles themselves are upgraded with cellular connectivity to transmit telemetry continuously.
explanation: Currently, only 200,000 of TerramEarth's 20 million vehicles (1%) have cellular connectivity, while 99% store telemetry locally until maintenance visits. Simply replacing FTP with streaming transport without expanding cellular connectivity leaves the vast majority of the fleet dark for weeks. Expanding fleet cellular connectivity to 80%, replacing batch FTP with real-time streaming ingestion, and applying machine learning to predict component failures directly solves the 3-week lag and reduces unplanned downtime below 1 week without inflating inventory carrying costs.

whyWrong.2: SFTP is still a batch file transfer protocol and does not solve either the batch delay or the lack of cellular connectivity across 99% of the fleet.
whyWrong.1: Migrating from FTP to streaming transport alone fails if 99% of vehicles remain unconnected to cellular networks and cannot stream data from the field.
whyWrong.3: Increasing dealer local inventory by a fixed factor directly violates TerramEarth's business requirement to reduce downtime without increasing the cost of carrying surplus inventory.

question: For this question, refer to the TerramEarth case study. Which of TerramEarth's legacy enterprise processes will experience significant change as a result of increased Google Cloud Platform adoption?
stem: For this question, refer to the TerramEarth case study. Which of TerramEarth's legacy enterprise processes will experience significant change as a result of increased Google Cloud Platform adoption?
options: Opex/Capex allocation, LAN changes, capacity planning
Capacity planning, TCO calculations, Opex/Capex allocation
Capacity planning, utilization measurement, data center expansion
Data center expansion, TCO calculations, utilization measurement
hint: Cloud adoption fundamentally transforms capacity planning (from hardware procurement to elastic autoscaling), TCO modeling, and CapEx-to-OpEx financial accounting.
explanation: Migrating from on-premises data centers to Google Cloud fundamentally transforms three core enterprise processes: capacity planning shifts from multi-year physical hardware procurement to elastic, on-demand scaling; Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) calculations shift from power, cooling, and rack space to managed service consumption; and financial budgeting shifts from upfront Capital Expenditure (CapEx) to pay-as-you-go Operating Expenditure (OpEx). Physical data center expansion is eliminated rather than transformed.

whyWrong.0: Local office LAN administration is largely unaffected by migrating backend data center workloads to Google Cloud.
whyWrong.2: Data center expansion is eliminated rather than modified when moving growth workloads to public cloud infrastructure.
whyWrong.3: Data center expansion is eliminated rather than transformed by cloud adoption.

topic: Resumable Uploads & Regional Storage Ingestion
question: For this question, refer to the TerramEarth case study. To speed up data retrieval, more vehicles will be upgraded to cellular connections and be able to transmit data to the ETL process. The current FTP process is error-prone and restarts the data transfer from the start of the file when connections fail, which happens often. You want to improve the reliability of the solution and minimize data transfer time on the cellular connections. What should you do?
stem: For this question, refer to the TerramEarth case study. To speed up data retrieval, more vehicles will be upgraded to cellular connections and be able to transmit data to the ETL process. The current FTP process is error-prone and restarts the data transfer from the start of the file when connections fail, which happens often. You want to improve the reliability of the solution and minimize data transfer time on the cellular connections. What should you do?
options: Use one Google Kubernetes Engine cluster of FTP servers. Save the data to a multi-regional bucket. Run the ETL process using data in the bucket.

Use multiple Google Kubernetes Engine clusters running FTP servers located in different regions. Save the data to multi-regional buckets in US, EU, and Asia. Run the ETL process using the data in the bucket.

Directly transfer the files to a different Google Cloud regional storage bucket location in US, EU, and Asia using Google APIs over HTTP(S). Run the ETL process to retrieve the data from each regional bucket.
Directly transfer the files to different Google Cloud multi-regional storage bucket locations in US, EU, and Asia using Google APIs over HTTP(S). Run the ETL process using the data in the bucket.
hint: Replace flaky FTP uploads with native Cloud Storage HTTPS resumable uploads into nearby regional buckets to minimize cellular round-trip latency and avoid restarting dropped transfers.
explanation: Native Google Cloud Storage JSON/XML APIs over HTTPS support resumable uploads out of the box, allowing intermittent cellular connections to resume from the last acknowledged byte chunk rather than restarting the entire file transfer. Uploading directly to regional Cloud Storage buckets located closest to the vehicles in the US, Europe, and Asia minimizes network round-trip time and cost compared to multi-regional buckets or maintaining custom FTP server clusters.

whyWrong.0: Retaining FTP servers keeps the exact protocol flaw where dropped cellular connections force full file restarts.
whyWrong.1: Running FTP clusters across regions still suffers from FTP transfer restarts over lossy cellular links and adds unnecessary GKE management overhead.
whyWrong.3: Regional buckets provide lower write cost and predictable single-region ingestion locality for regional ETL jobs compared to multi-regional buckets.

topic: Cost-Effective Multi-Region Big Data Processing
question: For this question, refer to the TerramEarth case study. TerramEarth's 20 million vehicles are scattered around the world. Based on the vehicle's location, its telemetry data is stored in a Google Cloud Storage (GCS) regional bucket (US, Europe, or Asia). The CTO has asked you to run a report on the raw telemetry data to determine why vehicles are breaking down after 100K miles. You want to run this job on all the data. What is the most cost-effective way to run this job?
stem: For this question, refer to the TerramEarth case study. TerramEarth's 20 million vehicles are scattered around the world. Based on the vehicle's location, its telemetry data is stored in a Google Cloud Storage (GCS) regional bucket (US, Europe, or Asia). The CTO has asked you to run a report on the raw telemetry data to determine why vehicles are breaking down after 100K miles. You want to run this job on all the data. What is the most cost-effective way to run this job?
options: Move all the data into one zone, then launch a Cloud Dataproc cluster to run the job.
Move all the data into one region, then launch a Google Cloud Dataproc cluster to run the job.
Launch a cluster in each region to preprocess and compress the raw data, then move the data into a multi-region bucket and use a Dataproc cluster to finish the job.
Launch a cluster in each region to preprocess and compress the raw data, then move the data into a regional bucket and use a Cloud Dataproc cluster to finish the job.
hint: Bring compute to the data: filter and compress raw telemetry inside each source region first to drastically reduce inter-region network egress charges.
explanation: Cross-continental network egress between Google Cloud regions (US, Europe, and Asia) is expensive when transferring petabytes of raw telemetry. By launching ephemeral Cloud Dataproc clusters in each source region to filter, aggregate, and compress the raw logs locally, you dramatically shrink the data volume before transferring the intermediate results into a single regional bucket where a final Dataproc cluster completes the global report. Using a regional destination bucket avoids the higher storage cost of a multi-region bucket.

whyWrong.0: Copying all raw uncompressed telemetry across continents into one zone incurs massive inter-region network egress charges.
whyWrong.1: Moving all raw uncompressed telemetry across regions before filtering wastes substantial money on inter-continental egress.
whyWrong.2: Storing the consolidated intermediate data in a multi-region bucket costs more than a regional bucket in the same region as the final Dataproc cluster.

topic: Coldline Storage for Offline ML Training Datasets
question: For this question, refer to the TerramEarth case study. TerramEarth has equipped unconnected trucks with servers and sensors to collect telemetry data. Next year, they want to use the data to train machine learning models. They want to store this data in the cloud while reducing costs. What should they do?
stem: For this question, refer to the TerramEarth case study. TerramEarth has equipped unconnected trucks with servers and sensors to collect telemetry data. Next year, they want to use the data to train machine learning models. They want to store this data in the cloud while reducing costs. What should they do?
options: Have the vehicle's computer compress the data in hourly snapshots and store it in a Google Cloud Storage (GCS) Coldline bucket.
Push the telemetry data in real time to a streaming Dataflow job that compresses the data, and store it in Google BigQuery.
Push the telemetry data in real time to a streaming Dataflow job that compresses the data, and store it in Cloud Bigtable.
Have the vehicle's computer compress the data in hourly snapshots and store it in a Google Cloud Storage (GCS) Nearline bucket.
hint: For unconnected vehicles whose telemetry will not be accessed until next year's ML training cycle, batch-compress snapshots locally and store them in Coldline storage.
explanation: Two constraints govern this design: the trucks are unconnected (eliminating any real-time streaming ingestion), and the data will not be read until next year's machine learning training project. Compressing hourly snapshots on the vehicle computer and uploading them during maintenance to a Cloud Storage Coldline bucket minimizes storage costs for data accessed less than once every 90 to 365 days.

whyWrong.3: Nearline storage is priced for data accessed roughly once a month and has higher per-GB storage costs than Coldline for data untouched until next year.
whyWrong.1: Unconnected trucks have no cellular link to push real-time streams to Dataflow.
whyWrong.2: Unconnected trucks cannot stream data in real time, and Cloud Bigtable is a high-cost low-latency NoSQL database unsuitable for cold archival.

topic: Edge ML Inference for Connected and Unconnected Fleets
question: For this question, refer to the TerramEarth case study. Operational parameters such as oil pressure are adjustable on each of TerramEarth's vehicles to increase their efficiency, depending on their environmental conditions. Your primary goal is to increase the operating efficiency of all 20 million cellular and unconnected vehicles in the field. How can you accomplish this goal?
stem: For this question, refer to the TerramEarth case study. Operational parameters such as oil pressure are adjustable on each of TerramEarth's vehicles to increase their efficiency, depending on their environmental conditions. Your primary goal is to increase the operating efficiency of all 20 million cellular and unconnected vehicles in the field. How can you accomplish this goal?
options: Have your engineers inspect the data for patterns, and then create an algorithm with rules that make operational adjustments automatically.
Capture all operating data, train machine learning models that identify ideal operations, and run locally to make operational adjustments automatically.
Implement a Google Cloud Dataflow streaming job with a sliding window, and use Google Cloud Messaging (GCM) to make operational adjustments automatically.
Capture all operating data, train machine learning models that identify ideal operations, and host in Google Cloud Machine Learning (ML) Platform to make operational adjustments automatically.
hint: Train ML models centrally in Google Cloud using fleet-wide telemetry, then deploy the trained models to run edge inference locally on each vehicle's onboard computer.
explanation: Because 99% of TerramEarth's 20 million vehicles operate without cellular connectivity in remote mines and farms, cloud-hosted real-time inference or streaming control loops cannot reach unconnected vehicles. Capturing telemetry across the fleet, training ML models in the cloud, and deploying those models onto the vehicles' onboard modules (via cellular updates or the maintenance port) enables real-time local parameter tuning across all 20 million connected and unconnected vehicles.

whyWrong.0: Hand-coded static rules cannot capture the complex multi-variable interactions across 120 sensor fields and diverse global operating environments.
whyWrong.2: Cloud streaming jobs and push notifications require continuous internet connectivity, which 99% of TerramEarth's vehicles lack.
whyWrong.3: Hosting inference exclusively in the cloud leaves unconnected vehicles unable to adjust operational parameters in the field.

topic: Zero-Trust Microservices & Hardware Root of Trust (TPM)
question: For this question, refer to the TerramEarth case study. Your agricultural division is experimenting with fully autonomous vehicles. You want your architecture to promote strong security during vehicle operation. Which two architectures should you consider? (Choose two)
stem: For this question, refer to the TerramEarth case study. Your agricultural division is experimenting with fully autonomous vehicles. You want your architecture to promote strong security during vehicle operation. Which two architectures should you consider? (Choose two)
options: Treat every microservice call between modules on the vehicle as untrusted.
Require IPv6 for connectivity to ensure a secure address space.
Use a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) and verify firmware and binaries on boot.
Use a functional programming language to isolate code execution cycles.
Use multiple connectivity subsystems for redundancy.
Enclose the vehicle's drive electronics in a Faraday cage to isolate chips.
hint: Combine hardware root-of-trust verified boot (TPM) with zero-trust mutual authentication between every onboard microservice.
explanation: Securing safety-critical autonomous vehicles requires defense in depth across hardware and software layers. First, a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) establishes a cryptographic root of trust that verifies firmware and binary signatures during secure boot so tampered code cannot execute. Second, treating every inter-module microservice call as untrusted (zero-trust architecture with mutual authentication) prevents lateral movement if any single onboard component is compromised.

whyWrong.1: IPv6 expands address space but does not inherently authenticate or secure inter-service or external communications.
whyWrong.3: Choosing a functional programming language is a software design preference and does not enforce system or network security.
whyWrong.4: Redundant connectivity subsystems improve availability and reliability, not security against tampering or intrusion.
whyWrong.5: A Faraday cage blocks external RF signals (preventing vehicle connectivity) without securing software execution or internal bus calls.

question: For this question, refer to the JencoMart case study. What Google domain and project structure should you recommend?
stem: For this question, refer to the JencoMart case study. The JencoMart security team requires that all Google Cloud Platform infrastructure is deployed using a least privilege model with separation of duties for administration between production and development resources. What Google domain and project structure should you recommend?
options: Create two G Suite accounts to manage users: one for development/test/staging and one for production. Each account should contain one project for every application.
Create two G Suite accounts to manage users: one with a single project for all development applications and one with a single project for all production applications.
Create a single G Suite account to manage users with each stage of each application in its own project.
Create a single G Suite account to manage users with one project for the development/test/staging environment and one project for the production environment.
hint: Manage corporate identities centrally in a single Google Workspace / Cloud Identity domain while isolating non-production and production workloads into separate GCP projects.
explanation: Google Cloud best practices recommend maintaining a single Google Workspace / Cloud Identity domain so user identities, groups, and SSO policies are governed centrally. Within that single organization, isolating non-production resources (development/test/staging) from production resources using distinct Google Cloud projects enforces hard IAM boundaries and separation of duties without creating unnecessary identity sprawl.

whyWrong.0: Splitting corporate users across multiple Google Workspace domains fragments identity governance and duplicates user administration.
whyWrong.1: Maintaining two separate Google Workspace domains is an anti-pattern that complicates IAM and centralized auditing.
whyWrong.2: Creating a separate project for every individual lifecycle stage of every application creates excessive administrative overhead compared to grouping non-production vs. production environments.

topic: Hybrid Migration Network & Compute Bottlenecks
question: For this question, refer to the JencoMart case study. The migration of JencoMart's application to Google Cloud Platform (GCP) is progressing too slowly. You want to maximize throughput. What are three potential bottlenecks? (Choose three)
stem: For this question, refer to the JencoMart case study. The migration of JencoMart's application to Google Cloud Platform (GCP) is progressing too slowly. You want to maximize throughput. What are three potential bottlenecks? (Choose three)
options: A single VPN tunnel, which limits throughput.
A tier of Google Cloud Storage that is not suited for this task.
A copy command that is not suited to operate over long distances.
Fewer virtual machines (VMs) in GCP than on-premises machines.
A separate storage layer outside the VMs, which is not suited for this task.
Complicated internet connectivity between the on-premises infrastructure and GCP.
hint: Hybrid VM migration throughput is typically constrained by single IPsec VPN tunnel caps (1.5-3 Gbps), public internet routing hops, and undersized target VM receiver fleets.
explanation: When migrating large on-premises workloads to Compute Engine over Cloud VPN, three infrastructure bottlenecks commonly restrict throughput: (1) a single Cloud VPN tunnel is capped at 1.5–3 Gbps per tunnel; (2) public internet transit between on-premises data centers and Google Cloud suffers from ISP hops, packet loss, and bandwidth contention; and (3) provisioning fewer receiving VMs in GCP than sending servers on-premises starves the ingestion side of CPU and network I/O capacity.

whyWrong.1: All Cloud Storage classes offer the same high ingestion throughput and millisecond access latency; storage class does not throttle upload speed.
whyWrong.2: Network bandwidth and tunnel limits dominate long-distance transfer throughput far more than the local copy utility.
whyWrong.4: Google Cloud Persistent Disks and Cloud Storage provide high-throughput decoupled storage designed specifically for cloud workloads.

topic: Non-Disruptive Troubleshooting of Unreachable GCE Instances
question: For this question, refer to the JencoMart case study. A few days after JencoMart migrates the user credentials database to Google Cloud Platform and shuts down the old server, the new database server stops responding to SSH connections. It is still serving database requests to the application servers correctly. What three steps should you take to diagnose the problem? (Choose three)
stem: For this question, refer to the JencoMart case study. A few days after JencoMart migrates the user credentials database to Google Cloud Platform and shuts down the old server, the new database server stops responding to SSH connections. It is still serving database requests to the application servers correctly. What three steps should you take to diagnose the problem? (Choose three)
options: Delete the virtual machine (VM) and disks and create a new one.
Delete the instance, attach the disk to a new VM, and investigate.
Take a snapshot of the disk and connect to a new machine to investigate.
Check inbound firewall rules for the network the machine is connected to.
Connect the machine to another network with very simple firewall rules and investigate.
Print the serial console output for the instance for troubleshooting, activate the interactive console, and investigate.
hint: Never delete or disrupt a live production database VM that is actively serving traffic; inspect VPC firewall rules, check the serial console, and clone the disk via snapshot to a forensic VM.
explanation: Because the credentials database is actively serving production authentication traffic under a 100% uptime SLA, any diagnostic action must be completely non-disruptive. First, verify VPC inbound firewall rules to ensure TCP port 22 is not blocked. Second, inspect the VM's serial console output and interactive serial console to diagnose OS/sshd issues without network SSH. Third, create a Persistent Disk snapshot, create a new disk from that snapshot, and attach it to a separate troubleshooting VM to inspect logs and configuration files offline.

whyWrong.0: Deleting the VM and disks destroys the production user credentials database and causes an immediate outage.
whyWrong.1: Deleting the running instance causes production downtime on a database with a 100% uptime SLA.
whyWrong.4: Reconfiguring network interfaces on a live production database risks severing active application database connections.

topic: NoSQL Document Database for User Profiles
question: For this question, refer to the JencoMart case study. JencoMart wants to migrate their user profile storage from their legacy 20 TB Oracle database to a managed Google Cloud database service that scales automatically and supports flexible user profile attributes. Which Google database should they use?
stem: For this question, refer to the JencoMart case study. JencoMart wants to migrate their user profile storage from their legacy 20 TB Oracle database to a managed Google Cloud database service that scales automatically and supports flexible user profile attributes. Which Google database should they use?
options: Google Cloud Spanner
Google BigQuery
Google Cloud Datastore (Firestore in Datastore mode)
Google Cloud SQL
hint: Cloud Datastore (Firestore in Datastore mode) is Google's fully managed, horizontally scalable NoSQL document database ideal for user profiles and session state.
explanation: User profile records are keyed by user ID and contain semi-structured, evolving attributes that do not require complex cross-table relational joins. Google Cloud Datastore (now Firestore in Datastore mode) provides serverless automatic horizontal scaling to tens of terabytes, low-latency key-value and document lookups, ACID transactions, and zero database administration overhead at a much lower cost than Cloud Spanner.

whyWrong.0: Cloud Spanner provides globally distributed relational SQL with external consistency, which is unnecessarily expensive for key-based user profile lookups.
whyWrong.1: BigQuery is an OLAP analytical data warehouse with high query latency unsuitable for low-latency OLTP user profile reads and writes.
whyWrong.3: Cloud SQL is a regional relational database with vertical scaling limits that is less flexible and harder to scale globally than Datastore for 20+ TB of user profiles.

topic: Hybrid Service Account Credential Management
question: For this question, refer to the JencoMart case study. JencoMart has decided to migrate user profile storage to Google Cloud Datastore and the application servers to Google Compute Engine (GCE). During the migration, the existing infrastructure will need access to Datastore to upload the data. What service account key management strategy should you recommend?
stem: For this question, refer to the JencoMart case study. JencoMart has decided to migrate user profile storage to Google Cloud Datastore and the application servers to Google Compute Engine (GCE). During the migration, the existing infrastructure will need access to Datastore to upload the data. What service account key management strategy should you recommend?
options: Provision service account keys for the on-premises infrastructure and for the GCE virtual machines (VMs).
Authenticate the on-premises infrastructure with a user account and provision service account keys for the VMs.
Deploy a custom authentication service on GCE/Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) for the on-premises infrastructure and use GCP-managed keys for the VMs.
Provision service account keys for the on-premises infrastructure and use Google Cloud Platform (GCP) managed keys for the VMs.
hint: Use Google-managed attached service accounts (metadata server tokens) for workloads running inside GCP, and only provision external credentials for on-premises workloads.
explanation: Workloads running on Compute Engine VMs should never use downloaded JSON service account key files; instead, they should use attached service accounts with Google-managed keys where short-lived OAuth2 tokens are automatically rotated and served via the local instance metadata server. For legacy on-premises servers outside GCP during migration, provisioning dedicated service account credentials enables programmatic authentication to Cloud Datastore.

whyWrong.0: Downloading static JSON service account keys onto GCE VMs creates an unnecessary credential leakage risk when Google-managed attached service accounts are available natively.
whyWrong.1: Automated server workloads must never authenticate with human user accounts, and GCE VMs should use Google-managed keys rather than static key files.
whyWrong.2: Building and maintaining a custom authentication broker is unnecessary operational overhead when IAM service accounts natively support both environments.

question: For this question, refer to the JencoMart case study. JencoMart has built a version of their application on Google Cloud Platform that serves traffic to Asia. You want to measure success against their business and technical goals. Which metrics should you track?
stem: For this question, refer to the JencoMart case study. JencoMart has built a version of their application on Google Cloud Platform that serves traffic to Asia. You want to measure success against their business and technical goals. Which metrics should you track?

Latency difference between US and Asia
Total visits, error rates, and latency from Asia
Error rates for requests from Asia
The number of character sets present in the database
hint: Pair the primary business adoption KPI (total visits from Asia) with the primary technical performance KPI (average latency for users in Asia).

question: An e-commerce company migrating from a co-located data center to Google Cloud has asked you to recommend machine types they should deploy their application servers to. Traffic peaks in the mornings and weekend evenings while sitting 80% idle at other times. How should you proceed?

Recommend deploying application servers to machine types that offer the highest RAM-to-CPU ratio available.
Recommend deploying into production with the smallest instances available, monitoring them over time, and scaling the machine type up until the desired performance is reached.
Identify the number of virtual cores and RAM associated with the application server virtual machines, align them to a custom machine type in the cloud, monitor performance, and scale up.
hint: Avoid carrying over on-premises over-provisioning: start with small, cost-effective instances in an autoscaled group, monitor actual cloud telemetry, and right-size upward as needed.
explanation: On-premises physical and virtual servers are typically sized for worst-case peak capacity plus multi-year growth buffers, leaving them idle 80% of the time. Directly mapping legacy hardware or VM specs into Compute Engine perpetuates expensive over-provisioning. Deploying with small instances, observing actual CPU/memory metrics in Cloud Monitoring under load, and scaling machine types until performance targets are met achieves optimal cost efficiency.

whyWrong.0: Mapping 1:1 from legacy physical hardware carries over severe on-premises over-provisioning (80% idle capacity) into cloud bills.
whyWrong.1: Blindly selecting high-memory machine types wastes money on unused RAM when workload memory requirements do not demand it.
whyWrong.3: Copying legacy on-premises VM allocations into custom machine types still imports historical over-provisioning rather than empirically right-sizing on cloud hardware.

topic: Zero-Downtime MySQL Migration with Asynchronous Replication
question: A company has asked you for advice on how to migrate their live on-premises MySQL deployment to Google Cloud. They want to minimize downtime and performance impact to their on-premises solution during the migration. Which approach should you recommend?
stem: A company has asked you for advice on how to migrate their live on-premises MySQL deployment to Google Cloud. They want to minimize downtime and performance impact to their on-premises solution during the migration. Which approach should you recommend?
options: Create a dump of the on-premises MySQL master server, shut it down, upload it to the cloud environment, and load it into a new MySQL cluster.
Create a dump of the MySQL replica server into the cloud environment, load it into Google Cloud Datastore, and configure applications to read/write to Cloud Datastore at cutover.
Create a new MySQL cluster in the cloud, configure applications to begin writing to both on-premises and cloud MySQL masters, and destroy the original cluster at cutover.
Set up a MySQL replica server/slave in the cloud environment, and configure it for asynchronous replication from the MySQL master server on-premises until cutover.
hint: Configure a cloud MySQL read replica using asynchronous binary log replication from the on-premises primary database so cutover requires only a brief write freeze.
explanation: Setting up a MySQL replica in Google Cloud configured for asynchronous replication from the on-premises primary database continuously streams binary log changes without blocking on-premises write transactions. Once the cloud replica catches up, cutover requires only a brief maintenance window to pause writes, let the final binlog events drain, and promote the cloud replica to primary.

whyWrong.0: Shutting down the primary database during a full dump, upload, and restore causes hours or days of complete application downtime.
whyWrong.2: Dual-writing to two active MySQL masters across a WAN introduces severe split-brain conflicts, auto-increment collisions, and data corruption.
whyWrong.1: Migrating from relational MySQL to NoSQL Cloud Datastore requires a complete application rewrite rather than a low-risk database migration.

stem: An operations team configured a new uptime check with Google Cloud Monitoring (Stackdriver) for several of their legacy web services. The Cloud Monitoring dashboard is not reporting the services as healthy even though external users can reach them. What should they do?
options: In the Google Cloud Console, download the list of the uptime servers' IP addresses and create an inbound firewall rule.
Install the Cloud Monitoring agent on all of the legacy web servers.
Configure their load balancer to pass through the User-Agent HTTP header when the value matches GoogleStackdriverMonitoring-UptimeChecks.
Configure their legacy web servers to allow requests that contain the User-Agent HTTP header when the value matches GoogleStackdriverMonitoring-UptimeChecks.
hint: Cloud Monitoring uptime probes originate from published Google IP ranges; allow those source IPs in your perimeter firewall so probes are not dropped.
explanation: Cloud Monitoring uptime checks probe public endpoints from distributed Google prober servers around the world. If perimeter or VPC firewalls block traffic from those prober IP ranges, uptime checks fail even when the application is running normally. Downloading Google's published uptime-check source IP ranges and adding an inbound firewall allow rule resolves the blocked health probes.

whyWrong.2: Load balancers already forward HTTP headers by default; network-layer firewall drops occur before HTTP header inspection.

Adding comprehensive unit tests validates isolated code paths, while running production-scale load tests against a cloud staging environment validates autoscaling policies, connection pools, and database throughput before cutover.

explanation: The standard cloud-native pattern for user-generated media separates binary blob storage from fast queryable metadata. Storing the raw images in Google Cloud Storage provides unlimited scale, high upload throughput, and signed URL access control. Storing the mapping between each customer ID, viewing permissions, and Cloud Storage object URIs in Cloud Datastore (Firestore) enables single-digit millisecond indexed queries when rendering a user's home page upon login.

Use a global load balancer with a set of virtual machines that forward the requests to a closer group of virtual machines managed by your operations team.

topic: Deterministic Encryption & PCI Tokenization Vault Architecture
question: For this question, refer to the Helicopter Racing League (HRL) case study. HRL's payment engineering team is designing a custom card tokenization vault for tens of thousands of season ticket holders and merchandise buyers. The vault must detect duplicate credit card submissions without storing plaintext PANs, support annual cryptographic key rotation, and minimize storage and lookup latency costs. Why is deterministic encryption stored in Firestore in Datastore mode preferred over probabilistic AEAD encryption or Cloud SQL column encryption?
stem: For this question, refer to the Helicopter Racing League (HRL) case study. HRL's payment engineering team is designing a custom card tokenization vault for tens of thousands of season ticket holders and merchandise buyers. The vault must detect duplicate credit card submissions without storing plaintext PANs, support annual cryptographic key rotation, and minimize storage and lookup latency costs. Why is deterministic encryption stored in Firestore in Datastore mode preferred over probabilistic AEAD encryption or Cloud SQL column encryption?
options: Deterministic encryption produces identical ciphertext for identical plaintext inputs under the same key version, enabling direct equality lookups in Firestore without decrypting every record.
Deterministic encryption automatically rotates underlying Cloud KMS hardware security module keys every 24 hours without re-encrypting stored ciphertexts.
Probabilistic AEAD encryption cannot be decrypted outside of Google Kubernetes Engine confidential nodes.
Firestore in Datastore mode automatically masks credit card numbers using built-in Cloud DLP inspection triggers at zero cost.
hint: Deterministic encryption maps identical card numbers to identical ciphertexts under a given key, enabling O(1) indexed duplicate detection in Firestore without storing plaintext.
explanation: Standard probabilistic encryption (AEAD) injects a random initialization vector (IV) on every encryption call, causing the same credit card number to yield a completely different ciphertext each time—making duplicate card detection impossible without scanning and decrypting the entire table. Deterministic encryption produces consistent ciphertext for identical plaintext under the active key version, allowing HRL's tokenization service to perform fast, low-cost indexed equality lookups in Firestore in Datastore mode while supporting annual key rotation via Cloud KMS key versions.

whyWrong.1: Cloud KMS key rotation is configured on a schedule (such as annually per HRL's requirement) and does not automatically re-encrypt existing database records every 24 hours.
whyWrong.2: Probabilistic AEAD encryption works across all compute environments; its limitation here is that random IVs prevent indexed equality queries for duplicate detection.
whyWrong.3: Firestore does not include free automatic Cloud DLP redaction triggers on writes.

topic: Cloud Armor Named IP Lists for Third-Party CDN Origin Protection
question: For this question, refer to the Helicopter Racing League (HRL) case study. To improve broadcast quality for fans in Cape Town, South Africa, HRL placed Fastly CDN in front of their Global External Application Load Balancer. The security team must ensure origin backends only accept requests proxied through Fastly and drop direct origin bypass attempts. Why must HRL use a Cloud Armor security policy with `evaluatePreconfiguredExpr('sourceiplist-fastly')` rather than VPC firewall rules?
stem: For this question, refer to the Helicopter Racing League (HRL) case study. To improve broadcast quality for fans in Cape Town, South Africa, HRL placed Fastly CDN in front of their Global External Application Load Balancer. The security team must ensure origin backends only accept requests proxied through Fastly and drop direct origin bypass attempts. Why must HRL use a Cloud Armor security policy with `evaluatePreconfiguredExpr('sourceiplist-fastly')` rather than VPC firewall rules?
options: VPC firewall rules cannot filter IPv4 CIDR blocks larger than a /24 prefix.

VPC firewall rules evaluate traffic at the VM network interface where source IPs are Google Front End (GFE) proxy addresses rather than the external CDN client IP, whereas Cloud Armor evaluates preconfigured CDN IP lists at the edge load balancer.
Cloud Armor security policies automatically establish BGP peering sessions with Fastly edge routers in Cape Town.
VPC firewall rules are stateless and cannot inspect TCP handshake packets arriving from external CDNs.
hint: External Application Load Balancers terminate client TCP connections at Google Front Ends (GFEs); use Cloud Armor named IP lists (`sourceiplist-fastly`) at the load balancer edge to filter upstream CDN IPs.
explanation: A Global External Application Load Balancer is a proxy-based Layer 7 load balancer implemented on Google Front Ends (GFEs). When traffic reaches backend VMs, the packet source IP is a GFE internal proxy range (`35.191.0.0/16` or `130.211.0.0/22`), not the original client or CDN IP. Cloud Armor operates directly at the GFE edge layer and provides Google-curated named IP lists (`sourceiplist-fastly`) that automatically stay synchronized whenever Fastly adds or retires edge CIDR blocks.

whyWrong.0: VPC firewall rules support arbitrary CIDR prefixes from `/0` to `/32`.
whyWrong.2: Cloud Armor is a WAF/DDoS policy engine at the load balancer layer and does not manage BGP routing sessions.
whyWrong.3: VPC firewall rules are stateful, not stateless; the architectural issue is proxy termination at the GFE.

stem: For this question, refer to the Helicopter Racing League (HRL) case study. HRL's development team deploys updates to their race prediction application every Tuesday at 03:00 UTC. The security team built an automated penetration testing Cloud Function named Airwolf that must execute immediately after each deployment finishes, even if build duration varies. Why should the deployment pipeline publish a completion event to Cloud Pub/Sub to trigger Airwolf instead of using a fixed Cloud Scheduler cron job at 03:00 UTC?
options: Cloud Pub/Sub automatically performs static code analysis on container images before delivering the trigger notification.
Cloud Scheduler cannot trigger Cloud Functions in the same VPC network as the deployment pipeline.

Publishing a deployment-completion message to Pub/Sub decouples the CI/CD pipeline from downstream security consumers and guarantees Airwolf tests the newly deployed release rather than racing against an in-progress rollout.
Cloud Functions triggered by Pub/Sub bypass IAM authentication checks against the target application.
hint: Trigger post-deployment security tests via an event published to Pub/Sub at the end of the deployment job so tests never start before rollout completion.
explanation: A fixed clock-based schedule (such as 03:00 UTC) creates a race condition: if a build or rollout takes longer than expected, the penetration test scans stale code or fails mid-rollout. Having the deployment pipeline emit a Pub/Sub notification upon successful rollout completion implements an event-driven choreography pattern that guarantees Airwolf runs immediately after the new version is live while allowing additional post-deploy subscribers to be added without modifying the pipeline.

whyWrong.1: Cloud Scheduler can invoke HTTP or Pub/Sub targets in any project or network configuration.
whyWrong.0: Cloud Pub/Sub is a messaging service and does not perform static code or container vulnerability scanning.
whyWrong.3: Pub/Sub triggers govern function invocation; outbound requests from the function still follow standard IAM and network controls.
